states_note: The per-issue, per-Run **Attempt lifecycle**, in order. It is a projection of the issue's **Strike** count against the Run's strike budget N (`max_strikes`, ADR-0070): no Strikes is `fresh`, 1 to N-1 is `retrying`, and N is `skipped`. Monotonic: Strikes are never refunded, so an issue only ever moves forward along this list, and only a new Run puts it back at the start. It is never written to the tracker -- a Run that demoted an issue there would be writing into the triage state machine it is only ever a consumer of, and one bad night would outlive the Run that had it.
strike_note: Every Session ending charges exactly one Strike to the issue the Session worked, and an advance charges none. Strikes are counted per issue: one issue's ending never moves another issue, and the Run never stops on Strikes -- it ends on a closed termination reason (`empty_pool`, `iteration_cap`, `all_skipped`, `all_blocked`, `operator_stop`) once no issue is left to work. An issue that is already `skipped` is charged nothing further, and `defeated_by` names the ending that charged its Nth Strike.

dispositions.note: The silent ending -- ran to the end, claimed no failure, left nothing behind -- is the shape a pair too cheap for the work fails in, so it is the one ending that also buys a harder pair for the retry its Strike leaves room for.

Charged like any other ending and retried while the issue has Strikes left (ADR-0070). It does not escalate: answering a wait that ran out with a slower, higher-reasoning pair near-guarantees a second timeout.

Evidence about the harness rather than about the work, so the pair does not move and the retry runs on the pair the issue already had. It still costs a Strike: something was spent, and N crashes on one issue in one Run are a pattern rather than an accident.

The Agent stating there is nothing to do. Charged and retried like any other ending until the issue's Strikes run out (ADR-0070): the declaration is often about the session's own view -- work already in an open PR, a misread ticket -- rather than about the issue, and a retry is how a Run tells the two apart. It does not escalate, because the dearest pair would be spent on work its worker says is absent.

A refused turn is a claim about the work, not about the pair, so it does not escalate; it is still retried while the issue has Strikes left. Routing a filtered session to a *different* model is deliberately out of scope: the generic rung would escalate a filtered turn into the model that filtered it.

advance_disposition.note: An Iteration that advanced its issue reached no ending at all, and the absence of one is not a sixth row. It charges no Strike, because the ledger counts failures to advance and work that lands is the opposite of one -- a ledger charged on every Iteration would defeat any issue whose work honestly takes N of them. It does not refund one either: an issue that advanced once under a Run that cannot finish it is the ordinary shape of a Run grinding, not evidence the Run recovered.

pickup_filter_note: A `skipped` issue is filtered out of the **Pickup** candidate list and never out of the **Pool**. The Pool stays whole -- the closure whitelist, the collection Event and the emptiness test are all computed over every eligible issue -- because filtering at collection would repeal the Pool-wide closure whitelist as a side effect: an Iteration working another issue could no longer close a defeated one by commit keyword, and a Run with open work in front of it would test as empty. Every Pickup seam an Orchestrator has honours it, reading the one lifecycle. Where a seam declines a candidate it had already chosen, the candidate is *declined*, so it leaves a `wrapper.pickup.skipped` record rather than silently vanishing. Where a seam's only decline returns the candidate to the list it was chosen from -- a released reservation, re-offered next turn -- the lifecycle narrows that list instead, because a decline re-taken every turn would emit one skip record per turn forever; the record the Run owes was already left by the seam that defeated the issue.

cases.note: A stall buys the rung and the retry to spend it on, and a second stall at the rung exhausts a budget of two.
The ending that moves one dial and not the other -- which is why the two are separate ledgers reading one ending, rather than one ledger answering both.

The ending #680 was defeated by in one Iteration under the Run-wide counter: its work sat in an open PR, the session said so, and the Run gave up on the issue. A retry is what lets a Run that has since seen the PR merge, or a session that reads the ticket differently, find work there.
The endings share one budget rather than each carrying their own, so an issue cannot alternate between them forever; the ending that charged the last Strike is the one recorded as the defeat.
The smallest budget the Runner accepts: no retry at all, which is the old outright-defeat disposition chosen by configuration rather than by ending.
One issue's endings never move another: a Strike is charged to the issue its session worked, so a Run can exhaust one issue and keep working the next with its whole budget intact.
Three productive Iterations in a row leave the issue exactly where it started, so an issue is worked as long as it keeps advancing.
Monotonic in the one shape where a refund would look reasonable: the escalated Iteration landed something, and the issue still has exactly one Strike left rather than a fresh budget.

Including against the ending that means the work landed. The lifecycle is a claim about this Run, and only a new Run withdraws it; a skipped issue is charged nothing further and keeps the ending that defeated it.

The two dials are independent in both directions. A Run whose rung is off -- disabled, or suppressed by an explicit model pin -- still stops re-picking an issue it cannot finish; it simply has no harder pair to try in between.
